Benedict Cooper.narrative: I am Benedict Cooper, and the barrels that carry this town's ale and berries are mine. My father was a cooper before me and I have kept the shed by the west wall these thirty years. Aethelred Tanner's leather bindings go on my barrels and he never lets me forget the debt. The stone road brings Kettlebridge hoops and their prices, and I pay the gate-due on every load like a fool.
values: a fair price for a fair barrel
goals: clear what I owe Aethelred Tanner
keep Baldwin Wade's custom at the Bell and Bush
see Martin made a master with his own mark

relations.name: Juliana Cooper
relations.label: wife
relations.note: She minds the stall and I mind the shed; between us the household stands.

relations.name: Martin Cooper
relations.label: son
relations.note: Quick with a plane, but he wants the master's mark before he has earned it.

relations.name: Baldwin Wade
relations.label: customer
relations.note: The Bell and Bush takes my barrels and pays on time; a good man to keep.

relations.name: Aethelred Tanner
relations.label: creditor
relations.note: I owe him for bindings and he counts every strap twice.

relations.name: Mercy Abbot
relations.label: guild head
relations.note: The Guild stall sells my wares; she wants the gate-due gone and I would not weep.

relations.name: Osric Abbot
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: A good hand with a bench; we talk wood and grumble at the due together.

relations.name: Wilfred Smith
relations.label: fellow tradesman
relations.note: Builds in timber like me, because stone costs the earth.

memories.gist: My father put the first plane in my hand and said a barrel that leaks is a lie.
The Lean Year: berries rotted in the fields and the barrels stood empty in my shed.
The day I took Martin on as apprentice and wrote his name in the book.
A Kettlebridge carter raised his hoop prices at the gate and I paid, because the ale must go out.
Juliana and I set up the stall in the square the spring after we wed.

stances.why: My name is on every cask; a leak is my shame.
Aethelred's bindings keep my barrels sound; I will not be a man who does not pay.
Every hoop and stave I bring in pays the due, and the price goes on my barrels.
I was years at the bench before my father let me sign a cask.

Juliana Cooper.narrative: I am Juliana Cooper and I mind the wooden-ware stall in the square: barrels, buckets, noggins, whatever Benedict and Martin turn out. I know what a thing is worth and I do not let a buyer talk me down twice. The stall pays the Guild its rent and the household eats because of it. I keep the house and the store and I count what comes in.
goals: sell off the small wares before winter
see Martin married to a decent trade
keep a little by against a bad year

relations.name: Benedict Cooper
relations.label: husband
relations.note: Slow to anger and slow to change; I do the talking at the stall.

relations.name: Martin Cooper
relations.label: son
relations.note: He wants to be a master at seventeen; he has not yet learned what a bad cask costs.

relations.name: Mercy Abbot
relations.label: guild head
relations.note: She takes the stall rent and sets the market terms; she is fair enough.

relations.name: Enid Fletcher
relations.label: fellow stallholder
relations.note: We watch each other's goods when one must step away.

relations.name: Petra Wade
relations.label: customer
relations.note: The inn buys our buckets and noggins; she counts the inn's store close.

relations.name: Aethelred Tanner
relations.label: creditor
relations.note: He holds Benedict's debt over us and I do not care for his manner.

relations.name: Cecily Carter
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: She sells eggs by my stall and we share the morning's gossip.

memories.gist: The first morning I spread our wares on the square and sold every bucket before noon.
The Lean Year: the square was thin and I sold a bucket for half what it was worth to feed the house.
Martin's first barrel came off the bench crooked and I sold it cheap to a farmer and said nothing.
A Kettlebridge carter sneered at my prices and I sent him off with nothing.

stances.why: The stall feeds us; a bad bargain is a hungry week.
I pay the stall rent and keep the market terms, whatever the guards do at the gate.
People buy from a household that pays its way.
Martin has skill but he has not yet earned the master's word.

Martin Cooper.narrative: I am Martin Cooper, seventeen, and I am apprenticed to my father at the cooper's bench. I can raise a barrel from staves and set a hoop true, and I am better at it than he was at my age, whatever he says. I want my own mark and my own shed, and I will not spend my life under his eye. The gate-due and the Kettlebridge price make everything dear, and I am sick of hearing of it.
values: my own name on a cask
not being spoken for by my father
goals: finish my indenture and be made a master
earn enough to set up my own bench
take a wife when I have a trade to keep her

relations.name: Benedict Cooper
relations.label: father
relations.note: He is a good cooper but he will not hear that I am ready.

relations.name: Juliana Cooper
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She sells my work at the stall and tells me true what it fetched.

relations.name: Baldwin Wade
relations.label: customer
relations.note: The inn's barrels come through my hands; he pays in coin and a word.

relations.name: Aethelred Tanner
relations.label: creditor
relations.note: His leather binds our barrels and he holds it over the house.

relations.name: Cedric Tanner
relations.label: friend
relations.note: He makes cart frames and wants to build in stone; we talk of a trade of our own.

relations.name: Stephen Hobson
relations.label: friend
relations.note: A mason's son who wants to build grander than a wall; good company at the inn.

memories.gist: The day my father let me set the hoops on a cask for the Bell and Bush and it held.
The Lean Year: no berries, no barrels, and I sat in the shed with nothing to do.
A carter told me my hoops were as good as any Kettlebridge work, and I have not forgotten it.
I watched Stephen Hobson's father lay a wall and thought I would rather build in wood and be my own master.

stances.why: I will not be a journeyman under my father's eye forever.
A cask that holds and is done by nightfall is a cask that sells.
Every stave I bring in costs more because of it, and my father just pays.
A man with no shed of his own has no business courting.
